journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: The Effect of Cervical Transcutaneous Vagus Nerve Stimulation on Word Memory in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Single-Blind Study
abstract: Purpose: The noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation has presented a promising adjunctive intervention in cognitive communication disorders. This randomized single-blind study aims to investigate the effect of cervical transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation (tVNS) on verbal memory in healthy adults. Method: Thirty-one participants were stratified into an experimental group ( n = 22) receiving 30-min cervical tVNS and a control group ( n = 9). Both groups completed a self-paced task to learn 50 Chinese words, followed by an immediate memory test and a 2-week delayed memory test assessing accuracy and reaction time (RT). Data of accuracy and RT were analyzed statistically based on tVNS stimulation, two sessions of memory test, and three age groups. Results: Cervical tVNS significantly improved memory performance, manifested in faster RT and higher accuracy compared to the control group, particularly for young adults. However, accuracy enhancement was age-specific: Only younger adults showed significantly improved recall accuracy with cervical tVNS, while middle-aged and older adults did not. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Adaptation to Auditory Errors Modulates Perception of the Errors
abstract: Purpose: Speakers adapt to auditory feedback perturbations by modifying their speech output. Although formant-clamp perturbations, in which feedback formants are fixed at predetermined values independent of the speaker's production, demonstrate that adaptation relies on the motor-to-auditory correspondence, it remains unclear how speakers perceive this feedback during adaptation. We hypothesized that if motor adaptation influences perception, then perceptual judgments of experience errors would change alongside adaptation, even when auditory feedback is held constant. Method: Thirty healthy adults performed an adaptation task across four conditions: formant-shift and formant-clamp perturbations, each introduced either suddenly or gradually. During each trial, participants produced consonant–vowel–consonant words and reported their perceived auditory feedback using a continuous vowel-identification slider. We quantified adaptive motor responses during the first 100 ms of the vowel and compared them with perceived errors derived from perceptual reports. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Shared Variance Across Cognitive Assessments Predicts Language Outcomes in Aphasia: A Preliminary Study
abstract: Purpose: Aphasia, a common consequence of stroke, often co-occurs with cognitive impairments, yet clinical assessment is limited by tools that are lengthy, linguistically demanding, and sometimes redundant. This preliminary study examined shared variance across widely used cognitive tests and explored how the resulting principal components related to aphasia severity and sentence comprehension efficiency. We also tested whether single tasks, those with the strongest component loadings, could predict language outcomes as effectively as the full component scores. Method: Seventeen adults with chronic aphasia and 21 matched controls completed the Test of Everyday Attention, the Cognitive Linguistic Quick Test-Plus, and the Visual and Auditory Duration Attention Network Tests. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify shared variance across cognitive tasks, followed by regression analyses relating components and single-task predictors to language outcomes. Results: PCA revealed six components, with subtests from the same battery generally clustering together, suggesting redundancy. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: A Randomized Comparative Effectiveness Trial of Many-Features and Few-Features Variants of Semantic Feature Analysis Treatment for Naming Impairment in Aphasia
abstract: Purpose: Semantic feature analysis (SFA) is a well-established and well-studied treatment for naming impairment in aphasia. Both theory and correlational evidence suggest that feature generation is a key active ingredient of the treatment. The purpose of this study was to test whether the number of features generated by participants in SFA is causally related to outcomes. Method: Forty-one individuals with aphasia due to left-hemisphere stroke of at least 6 months postonset were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either a many-features variant of SFA in which they were asked to generate 11 features per trial or a few-features variant in which they were asked to generate five features per trial. The entire study team, except for three treating clinicians, was blind to group assignment. Random group assignments were stratified by aphasia severity, blocked in groups of four, generated a priori by a team-external consultant, and managed by a treating clinician. One participant dropped out of the study following randomization, and the remaining participants were assessed twice prior to receiving 42 hr of SFA over 3 weeks, at treatment exit, and at 2- to 3-month follow-up. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Automatic Prediction of Vocal Strain Scores in Singing Voice Using Audio and Electroglottographic Modalities
abstract: Purpose: This study developed machine learning models to predict perceptual strain scores in the singing voice using audio and electroglottographic (EGG) recordings. The study examined the predictive capability of distinct feature sets extracted from audio and EGG modalities and assessed the contributions of participant metadata (META) and feature selection to model performance. Method: Data were split into mutually exclusive train-validation ( n = 16 singers, n ≈ 450 samples) and independent test ( n = 11 singers, n ≈ 240 samples) sets to ensure singer-independent generalization. Extracted features included mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, extended Geneva minimalistic acoustic parameter set, wavelet scattering coefficients, and domain-specific descriptors (audio: amplitude modulation; EGG: glottal dynamics), along with singer META. Using leave-one-singer-out cross-validation, we trained regression models (support vector regressor, random forest, and ridge) to predict the expert strain ratings. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Eye Tracking in Visuoperceptual Diagnostic Tasks in Health Care: A Scoping Review and Thematic Synthesis With Implications for Speech-Language Pathology
abstract: Purpose: Eye tracking provides objective measurement of visuoperceptual behavior during diagnostic interpretation. Although widely used in health care research, little is known about how speech-language pathologists (SLPs) visually engage with dynamic imaging. This scoping review mapped current research on clinicians' gaze behavior during visuoperceptual diagnostic tasks and synthesized methodological trends, outcome themes, and limitations to inform future speech-language pathology–focused eye-tracking research. Method: Following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines, five databases were searched for studies published between January 2000 and September 2025. Ninety-three studies met inclusion criteria. Data were extracted on study characteristics, diagnostic task characteristics, eye-tracking methodology, gaze outcomes, and reported limitations. Descriptive statistics summarized methodological features, and thematic analysis synthesized outcome trends and barriers. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Are Bilingual Children With Speech, Language, and Communication Needs More at Risk for Heritage Language Attrition Than Their Typically Developing Peers?
abstract: Purpose: We examined the language environment and proficiency of bilingual children with typical development (TD) and with speech, language, and communication needs (SLCNs). We asked whether the children with SLCNs had more reduced heritage language (HL) experiences than did their TD peers and whether this was associated with a weaker HL and a stronger societal language (SL). Method: Children ( N = 48, M age = 7.89 years) with TD and with SLCNs and their parents participated in this study; all were learning English as their SL with diverse HLs. Parents responded to a detailed questionnaire (Quantifying Bilingual Experience). Children completed a sentence repetition task in English. Results: The SLCN group had more lifetime input and output in the SL than in the HL, but the TD group showed the opposite pattern. The SLCN group had more current SL input and a less rich HL environment than did the TD group. The SLCN group was less willing to use their HL and had lower HL proficiency compared with the TD group. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Perceived Naturalness and Acoustic Characteristics of Habitual Versus Clear Speech for Individuals With Hearing Loss
abstract: Purpose: This study examined the impact of clear speech on perceived naturalness. We compared habitual speech (HS), untrained clear speech (UCS), and clear speech after a brief training (trained clear speech [TCS]) and examined whether acoustic variables differed between conditions and predicted naturalness. Method: Twelve adult female talkers read sentences in three conditions (HS, UCS, TCS). Twenty-eight normal-hearing adults rated naturalness on a 1–9 scale. Along with naturalness, acoustic measures of speech rate, number of pauses, and pause duration were obtained and compared between speaking conditions via linear mixed-effects models (LMMs). A slower speech rate and increased pausing were associated with inferior naturalness ratings, although these features may not fully explain the reduced naturalness of TCS. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Neural Correlates of the Acceptable Noise Level and Self-Reported Listening Skills in Young Adults With Autism Spectrum Disorder
abstract: Purpose: This brain–behavior study investigated the relationship between auditory sensory gating and noise acceptance in listeners with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Relationships between self-reported listening skills and auditory sensory gating were also examined. Method: Neural responses to pure-tone stimuli were elicited using a traditional, passive gating paradigm in 12 listeners with ASD and 12 neurotypical control listeners. Noise acceptance was quantified in all listeners using the acceptable noise level (ANL) measure. Self-reported listening abilities were measured using the Speech, Spatial, and Qualities of Hearing Scale (SSQ). Relationships between neural and behavioral measures were analyzed using linear mixed-effects regression. Results: Listeners with ASD accepted less noise when listening to concurrent speech, had higher intensity most comfortable levels for speech, and reported significantly more difficulties on the SSQ compared to the control group. Regression analyses showed that, across groups, weaker P1 gating was associated with poorer noise acceptance. title: Multimodal Language Processing in Children With Developmental Language Disorder: The Influence of Verbal and Visuospatial Memory
abstract: Purpose: This study investigates how verbal and visuospatial memory capacities contribute to the processing and comprehension of pragmatic meanings that are expressed multimodally in children with and without developmental language disorder (DLD). Method: Seventy-seven children (33 with DLD, 44 typically developing [TD]), aged 5–10 years, completed standardized memory tasks and participated in a visual-world eye-tracking experiment assessing both online processing and offline comprehension of sentences with simple and complex pragmatic meanings (interrogativity and indirect requests, respectively). Sentences were presented under three conditions: baseline (no prosodic nor gestural cues to target meanings), prosodically enhanced (target meanings enhanced through prosodic cues), and multimodally enhanced (target meanings enhanced through prosodic and gestural cues). Results: In accordance with previous findings, children with DLD showed significantly lower verbal and visuospatial memory scores than their TD peers, with more pronounced difficulties in the verbal domain. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Acoustic and Perceptual Speech Production Differences in Preschoolers With a History of Late and Typical Talking
abstract: Purpose: While an emerging body of research has demonstrated that late talkers (LTs) show continued subclinical deficits in language abilities, less is known about their development of speech production skills. The current study investigated speech production abilities among 3-year-old children with a history of late talking (hLTs) or typical talking (hTTs) using three measures of speech production skills. Method: We assessed speech production skills in a sample of 3-year-old children who were previously identified as LTs or typical talkers (44 hTTs, 31 hLTs) using a norm-referenced assessment of articulation abilities, a caregiver-report measure of speech intelligibility, and fine-grained acoustic analyses of both earlier- and later-acquired speech contrasts. We compared groups using continuous measures of performance. Results: Across all three measurement methods/types, hLTs showed poorer speech production skills compared to hTTs. Conclusions: This study demonstrates that, like on measures of lexical and syntactic development, hLTs experience subclinical differences in speech production skills during the preschool period. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Characterizing the Speech Breathing Kinematics of Older Adults With Presbyphonia
abstract: Background: Age-related changes to laryngeal and respiratory systems contribute to presbyphonia, yet the speech breathing behaviors that accompany or exacerbate ageing voice problems remain poorly characterized. This study examined speech breathing kinematics in older adults with presbyphonia and compared them with published data from vocally healthy peers. Method: Thirty-five adults with presbyphonia (20 men, 15 women; M age = 79.8 years) completed reading and monologue tasks in comfortable and background noise conditions while inductive plethysmography and calibrated acoustics were recorded. Primary outcome was lung volume initiation (LVI) expressed as % vital capacity (%VC) relative to end-expiratory level. Secondary measures included lung volume termination (LVT), lung volume excursion (LVE), LVE per syllable, expiratory flow, inspiratory flow, utterance length, rate of speech, and sound pressure level. Group and noise condition comparisons were made against normative cohorts using two-sample t tests and descriptive comparisons; mixed-effects models assessed utterance length effects. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: The Effect of Between-Ear Speech Perception Asymmetry on Localization, Spoken Language, and Literacy for Adolescents With Cochlear Implants
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to examine the effects of between-ear speech perception asymmetry on localization, spoken language, and reading in adolescents with early cochlear implants (CIs). Method: Eighty adolescents, who have long-term bilateral device use, participated: 10 with bimodal (BM) devices (CI plus hearing aid at the nonimplanted ear) and 70 with bilateral CIs (BCIs; 14 simultaneous, 56 sequential). Participants completed localization, unilateral speech perception, receptive language, and reading tests. Principal component analysis created composite scores for better-ear speech perception and between-ear speech perception asymmetry. Hierarchical regression examined the effects of demographics, audiological factors, and asymmetry on outcomes. Results: Localization scores for the two BCI groups did not differ significantly. Both BCI groups' localization scores were, however, significantly better than those of the BM group. Language and reading scores were not significantly different for the three groups. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Effect of Vowel Type on Aerodynamic Measures of Estimated Subglottal Pressure and Airflow
abstract: Introduction: The purpose of this study was to investigate the potential effect of factors such as tongue height and advancement and vocal tract constrictions on aerodynamic measures of voice (mean airflow [MAF] and estimated subglottal pressure [Psub]). A key question was whether the choice of elicitation vowel would have a substantial impact on normative expectations and subsequent clinical decision making that may be based on measures of MAF or Psub. Method: Forty-three nondysphonic male ( n = 13) and female ( n = 30) participants between the ages of 18 and 30 years were tested using the Phonatory Aerodynamic System (Model 6600, Pentax Medical Inc.). MAF was measured from sustained vowels /i/, /u/, and /α/ in their comfortable pitch and loudness using the comfortable sustained phonation protocol. MAF and Psub were also measured from repetitions of the syllable /pV/, where V was the target vowel (/i, u, α/. Measurement of vocal fundamental frequency ( F 0) during vowel production in the aforementioned protocols was also measured. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Contribution of Phonological Information to Lexical Access in School-Age Children With Cochlear Implants
abstract: Purpose: This study explores the interplay of phonological and lexical processing in children, focusing on whether German-speaking school-age children with cochlear implants (CIs) use phonological information for lexical access in the same way as their peers with typical hearing (TH). The study aimed at understanding how different phonological contrasts between a target and a phonological competitor affect lexical access when this acoustic information is less available, as is the case with CIs. Method: Using an eye-tracking visual-world paradigm, we hypothesized that lexical access would differ for the children with CIs due to their shorter hearing experience and/or the characteristics of the auditory input provided by the implants. We further hypothesized that processing the difference between a target and its phonological competitor would depend on the types and number of contrasting features available. Results: Our results show that (a) lexical access is slowed down in children with CIs when compared to their peers with TH, (b) not all phonological contrasts are used similarly in lexical access in both groups, and (c) individual factors do not explain these effects in this study

journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Predictors of Word Learning With and Without Retrieval Practice in Children With Developmental Language Disorder
abstract: Purpose: Both children with developmental language disorder (DLD) and their peers with typical language development (TD) vary in their response to word learning activities, even when a consistent procedure is used. In this study, we examine child factors that might help explain this variation in outcomes and whether any interaction between these factors operates in the same way as a function of whether retrieval practice is included in the word learning procedure. Method: We examined the relations between a common set of child factors and children's responses in five previously published novel word learning studies with similar procedures. Participants were 4- and 5-year-old English-speaking children with DLD and their same-age peers with TD. Factors included scores on standardized language and nonverbal intelligence tests, nonword repetition, maternal education, age, and group status (TD, DLD). The role of each factor was examined while controlling for the other factors. Results: With all other factors controlled, age proved to be predictive of children's novel word learning. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Neural Indicators of Inhibition in Tinnitus: Onset–Offset and Sensory Gating Auditory Evoked Potentials Vary by Stimulus Frequency and Tinnitus Severity
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of stimulus frequency and tinnitus severity on measurements indicative of inhibition called onset–offset and sensory gating auditory evoked potentials (AEPs). The specific aims were to (a) determine the effect of stimulus frequency on AEPs in people with and without tinnitus; (b) determine if people with high-frequency tinnitus demonstrate abnormal AEPs in response to high-frequency stimuli; and (c) compare AEPs in people with tinnitus of varying severity. Method: A total of 26 people with tinnitus and 26 age-, sex-, and hearing-matched no-tinnitus controls participated. AEPs were recorded in response to stimuli of varying frequency (broadband noise [BBN], 0.25, 2, 8 kHz). AEPs were quantified by measuring difference wave amplitudes and latencies. For Aims 1 and 2, mixed-model ANOVAs were calculated to determine the main effect of and interaction between stimulus frequency and tinnitus presence. For Aim 3, participants were divided into subgroups based on median tinnitus severity and t tests were used to compare AEPs between subgroups. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Characterizing Submental Neuromuscular Activity of Swallowing Rehabilitation: An Electromyographic Evaluation of Rehabilitative Maneuvers in Healthy Adults
abstract: Purpose: The effortful swallow (ES), the Mendelsohn maneuver (MM), and isometric tongue presses (TPs) are widely used swallowing maneuvers/exercises to improve elements of swallowing, such as muscle strength and biomechanics. However, the underlying neuromuscular mechanisms of these exercises remain unclear, potentially limiting our ability to specify treatment targets and improve treatment efficacy. This study aimed to compare submental neuromuscular activation patterns during the ES, MM, TPs, and typical swallows in healthy young and older adults. Method: As part of a larger randomized crossover validation study, 60 healthy adults (30 young and 30 older) completed typical swallows and three maneuvers using a wearable submental surface electromyographic (sEMG) system (i-Phagia). Outcome variables included (a) normalized mean sEMG amplitude and (b) time to peak sEMG amplitude. Linear mixed models were used to examine effects of task, age, and sex on both outcomes. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Characterizing Caregiver–Child Interactions Through a Transactional Lens: A Baseline Analysis of a Caregiver-Implemented Intervention
abstract: Purpose: This study was motivated by the transactional model of development and examined the reciprocal influences that children and caregivers have on caregiver–child interactions (CCXs) prior to a caregiver-implemented intervention. We tested whether child communication characteristics were associated with caregiver strategy use and whether these strategies, in turn, influenced children's communication to understand how caregivers and children mutually shaped the language learning environment. Method: Caregiver–child dyads ( N = 105) were participants in a randomized controlled trial. CCXs were collected when children were approximately 30 months of age, transcribed, and coded for four caregiver language facilitation strategies and child communication variables. Results: Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator regression and postselection inference indicated that child communication characteristics in CCXs were associated with both the frequency and type of strategies caregivers used. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods Study of the Effectiveness of the Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS): Part 2 of a CDMS Hybrid Effectiveness–Implementation Study
abstract: Purpose: As Part 2 of a Type 1 hybrid effectiveness–implementation study, we evaluated the effectiveness of the Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS), a validated pediatric dysphagia outcomes assessment completed by therapists following instrumental swallow assessments. Method: Guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance and Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research implementation science frameworks, mixed methods were used to evaluate CDMS effectiveness in a tertiary care children's hospital system across the following areas: general/workflow, referrals, follow-up care, communication, and patient/caregiver impact. Using an explanatory sequential design, quantitative results informed qualitative interview guides. Referrals for and receipt of dysphagia management follow-up care were evaluated for patients seen pre–CDMS implementation ( n = 533) and post–CDMS implementation ( n = 594). Separate analyses were conducted for patients with Down syndrome. Results were modeled via ordinal logistic regression across patient-level and contextual factors. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Academic English Language Screeners: Gatekeepers for Multilingual Learners
abstract: Purpose: This article describes the gatekeeping nature of academic English language screeners for multilingual learners. It highlights inequities in current English learner identification practices, advocates for universal academic language screening, and emphasizes the need for teacher training to support academic language development for all students, regardless of home language background. Conclusion: The article argues that more equitable and comprehensive identification practices, paired with strengthened teacher training, are essential to ensure that all students receive appropriate language support and are not disadvantaged by current screening systems.

journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Neural Processing of Phoneme Changes: Differences Between Children and Adults
abstract: Purpose: This study examined neural differences in processing of phoneme changes between 5- and 6-year-old Chinese–English bilingual young children and adults using a passive oddball task and event-related potentials. Method: Natural speech stimuli with digital refinement were used. Two syllables differing in vowels were manipulated: /da/ (the standard) and /di/ (the deviant). Results: The mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a were elicited by /di/ relative to /da/ in both the young child and adult groups. However, young children showed a reduced MMN, indicated by smaller mean amplitudes and later peak latencies, compared with adults, although peak-amplitude differences were not statistically significant. Young children also exhibited a significantly enhanced P3a (both mean amplitude and peak amplitude) alongside a delayed peak latency relative to adults. Notably, young children elicited a robust late mismatch response, manifesting as a significant positivity, whereas adults showed no significant response. Conclusion: These findings indicate maturational differences in early auditory change detection and involuntary attention orienting during phoneme processing. Supplemental Material:

journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Lexical Bias During Speech Perception Increases Under Signal Degradation but Not Cognitive Load
abstract: Purpose: Lexical information shapes the interpretation of ambiguous speech sounds, often biasing perception toward real words rather than nonwords—a phenomenon known as lexical bias. This study examined the extent to which signal degradation and cognitive load modulate this bias. Method: Younger adults with normal hearing categorized stimuli along two word–nonword continua (Bap/Gap and Back/Gack), which differed primarily in the formant transitions of the initial consonant. Stimuli were either unprocessed or vocoded to introduce signal degradation, simulating cochlear implant listening. Cognitive load was manipulated via a dual-task paradigm: Participants memorized digits (Experiment A) or images (Experiment B) under low- and high-cognitive-load conditions while performing the categorization task. Results: Across both experiments, participants demonstrated robust lexical bias and reported more “Gap” (word) responses for the Bap/Gap continuum and more “Back” (word) responses for the Back/Gack continuum. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Low-Intensity Distortion Product Otoacoustic Emission Protocols in Infants and Young Children: Contributions of Age-Specific Ear Characteristics
abstract: Purpose: Despite almost complete cochlear maturity at birth, distortion product otoacoustic emission (DPOAE) levels in neonates and infants are typically higher than those measured in older children and adults, depending on the type and frequency stimulus, which suggests functional immaturity of the cochlea as well as the role of the outer and/or middle ear. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between outer and middle ear characteristics, using wideband tympanometry (WBT), and DPOAEs and to evaluate the applicability of normative criteria at reduced stimulus intensities in children aged between 6 days and 5 years. Method: A total of 109 ears from 60 participants were examined and categorized into three age groups: newborns, infants (6–8 months), and children (3–5 years). The following measurements were analyzed: ear canal volume, compensated acoustic admittance (with 1-kHz probe tone and 226-Hz probe tone), acoustic absorbance, and DPOAEs with two stimulus intensity protocols ( L 1 – L 2 = 65–55 and 55–45 dB SPL). Statistical analyses included nonparametric tests and correlation models. Results: WBT measures reflect the age-related maturation of the conductive pathway.

journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Connecting Preschoolers' Spontaneous Speech Patterns to Future Language Skills: A 3-Year Concurrent and Longitudinal Cohort Study of Canonical Proportion as a Developmental Index
abstract: Purpose: Understanding how children's spontaneous language behavior relates to standardized metrics of speech and language remains a crucial challenge in studies of language acquisition and clinical assessment. Traditional lab- and clinic-based paradigms are time- and resource-intensive and may not fully capture a child's underlying language competencies. This study aimed to investigate whether automated analysis of naturalistic, child-centered audio recordings can index the developmental trajectory of speech-language abilities from 2 to 5 years of age. Method: A longitudinal design was employed with N = 155 preschoolers, who were followed from 2 to 5 years of age. Deep learning speech classification methods were used to compute canonical proportion—the proportion of a child's speech that is produced as canonical syllables (well-formed syllables with a consonant–vowel transition, such as “ba”), a key marker of speech motor control development and phonological representation building—from child-centered audio recordings collected at 2–4 years of age. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Short-Term Neurobehavioral Effects of Acute Respiratory Illness on Auditory–Motor Integration During Speech Production
abstract: Purpose: COVID-19 is an acute respiratory illness that has been shown to impair speech and voice, yet its effects on the neural dynamics of speech production remain largely unknown. This longitudinal study investigated the short-term neurobehavioral impact of COVID-19 on sensorimotor control of speech production. Method: Before and after COVID-19 infection, participants in the experimental group produced sustained vowels while hearing their voice unexpectedly pitch-shifted in auditory feedback. An age- and sex-matched control group without intervening COVID-19 infection underwent identical testing across a comparable interval. Vocal compensations and event-related potentials (ERPs), together with source localization and Granger causality analyses, were used to characterize the neurobehavioral effects of COVID-19 on vocal feedback control. Results: Compared to pre-infection state, the experimental group exhibited reduced vocal compensations, decreased N1 amplitudes, and increased P2 amplitudes with shortened latencies at post-infection state. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Efficient Language Sampling for Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children: Evaluating Reliability Across Length, Timing, and Context
abstract: Purpose: Given the time demands of language sample analysis, this study aimed to identify efficient, flexible sampling procedures that maintain strong reliability. We examine how language sample length in minutes, timing (i.e., beginning vs. later in the elicitation task following a warm-up period), and elicitation context (i.e., play or conversation) influence the reliability of four common language measures in young deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children. Method: Participants included 21 DHH children (3–5 years old) who completed 10-min play and conversation samples in English. Samples were transcribed and analyzed for mean length of utterance in words, mean length of utterance in morphemes, total number of words per minute, and number of different words per minute. We evaluated the reliability of these measures by comparing shorter segments (i.e., 1, 3, 5, and 7 min) to the full sample using Cronbach's alpha, with additional comparisons based on the sample's timing and elicitation context. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Fundamental Frequency and Noise Effects on Sentence Recognition in Mandarin-Speaking Autistic Children: The Role of Cognitive Abilities
abstract: Purpose: Previous studies have shown that Mandarin-speaking autistic children exhibit atypical pitch processing and their speech perception is easily affected by noise. This study examined how fundamental frequency ( F 0) contour and background noise affect Mandarin sentence recognition in autistic children, and evaluated the roles of verbal intelligence (VIQ), nonverbal intelligence (NVIQ), and working memory (WM) as cognitive predictors. Method: Thirty Mandarin-speaking autistic children and 31 age-matched typically developing (TD) controls completed an open-set sentence recognition task under four conditions: natural F 0 (NF0) versus flat F 0 (FF0) in quiet and in speech-shaped noise at 10 dB SNR. Performance was scored as percent correct monosyllables. VIQ and NVIQ were assessed using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale, and WM was assessed via forward digit span. Results: Both the ASD and TD groups showed reduced accuracy when F 0 contours were flattened and in the presence of noise. The performance of autistic children declined disproportionately under FF0 conditions, whereas they matched TD peers when the F 0 was natural. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Interactive Effects of Executive Function and Language Ability on Children's Cross-Situational Word Learning
abstract: Purpose: This study examined whether executive function (EF) skills predict cross-situational word learning (CSWL) in children and whether EF–CSWL relationships vary as a function of language ability, including in children with developmental language disorder (DLD). Method: Fifty monolingual English-speaking children 5–9 years of age completed a CSWL task in which they learned five novel words. EF was measured using indices derived from the dimensional change card sort task, indexing shifting, inhibitory control, and monitoring skills. Results: EF skills predicted CSWL, but critically, language ability moderated these effects. Specifically, statistical word learning performance improved as shifting and monitoring skills increased, but only in children with average-to-high language skills. Weaker EF skills attenuated the benefit of language ability on statistical word learning in children with robust language systems. Across models, EF explained little variance in CSWL performance in children with weaker language skills, including those with DLD. title: MyCommunication-Adults: Psychometric Properties of a New Generic Communicative Participation Measure for People With Communication Problems and Development of Short Forms
abstract: Purpose: A preliminary item bank of 133 items from MyCommunication-Adults, a patient-reported outcome measure focusing on communicative participation, underwent content validity testing to ensure its relevance, comprehensibility, and comprehensiveness. The present study aimed to assess the structural validity, construct validity, and reliability of MyCommunication-Adults and develop short forms for clinical use. Method: Adults with communication problems completed the full MyCommunication-Adults item bank, the Dutch Communicative Participation Item Bank (CPIB) short form (measuring communicative participation), and the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System v2.0 Short Form 8a – Ability to Participate in Social Roles and Activities (PROMIS-APS; measuring general participation). The psychometric properties of MyCommunication-Adults were assessed using confirmatory factor analysis, item response theory analyses, and Pearson correlations. Results: A total of 500 adults with communication problems participated. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Multi-Atlas–Based Segmentation of Pediatric Vocal Tract Anatomy in Dynamic Magnetic Resonance Imaging
abstract: Purpose: Segmentation of velopharyngeal and vocal tract anatomy is crucial for quantifying structures and analyzing dynamics during speech. Automatic methods are needed to replace labor-intensive and poorly reproducible manual segmentation. To address this, we compared four multi-atlas–based methods to determine which provides the most accurate segmentation of the tongue, velum, and adenoid and how segmentation accuracy varies with the number of temporal frames. Method: Five spatiotemporal atlases of speech tasks were built, each with around 80 frames. We performed diffeomorphic registration of 10–40 frames of each atlas, then propagated labels to evaluate how the number of frames impacts performance. Four label fusion techniques—majority voting label fusion (MVLF), simultaneous truth and performance level estimation (STAPLE), multi-atlas label fusion (MALF), and corrective learning (CL)—were applied to evaluate segmentation accuracy. Performance was assessed using dice similarity coefficient (DSC) values across increasing numbers of input frames (10–40). journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Adolescents Activate Phonology When Reading Familiar Words
abstract: Purpose: A central debate in reading research is how phonology functions in written word recognition. There are different perspectives, from the idea that phonology is automatically engaged to access word meaning (prelexical coding) to the opposing view that phonology plays no role in meaning activation (postlexical coding). To tease apart these perspectives, we employed a newly developed written word version of the visual world paradigm (VWP) to measure the real-time activation of phonology during familiar-word reading in adolescents. Method: A total of 30 monolingual adolescents aged 11–14 years were tested using a novel written word version of the VWP. In this paradigm, participants saw four pictures on a screen and clicked the picture of the word they read (e.g., “BAT”) while their eye movements were tracked. Pictures represented the target word (e.g., “BAT”), two unrelated words (e.g., “HOOF,” “MILK”), and an anadrome (e.g., “TAB”). Anadromes, which can be orthographic and phonological such as “BAT”–“TAB,” orthographic such as “LEG”–“GEL,” or phonological such as “JAB”–“BADGE,” separate phonology from orthography. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Development of the Receptive and Expressive Vocabulary of Children in Different Care Settings: A Longitudinal Exploration
abstract: Purpose: Language development in children is influenced by both environmental and individual factors. This study examined vocabulary development among children in care, longitudinally considering environmental (different care types) and individual (temperament) factors. Method: A total of 211 children under social services care in different care types in Türkiye (23–61 months old, n boys = 126, n girls = 85), together with their caregivers and foster families, were assessed three times at 8-month intervals. Information about the care history of the children and day care attendance was included in the analysis. Temperament was assessed using the Early Childhood Behavior Questionnaire and the Children's Behavior Questionnaire. Vocabulary scores were measured with the Turkish Expressive and Receptive Language Test. Results: Hierarchical linear models revealed that vocabulary skills improved over time across all care types. However, the growth rate of receptive vocabulary was negatively associated with the duration of time spent in care. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Conversational–Communicative Experience and Theory of Mind in Taiwanese Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children
abstract: Purpose: This study examined theory-of-mind (ToM) development in Taiwanese deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children with early hearing provisions, extending prior evidence from Western contexts. We specifically tested whether conversational–communicative experience, indexed by DHH children's accumulated hearing experience, predicts ToM through language competence and explored what ToM sequence characterizes Taiwanese DHH children. Method: Sixty-five DHH children (4–6 years of age) with cochlear implants or hearing aids and 65 chronological age-matched hearing peers were tested for their ToM and language. All children were monolingual speakers of Mandarin growing up in Taiwan. We used structural equation modeling to examine the pathways linking accumulated hearing experience, language, and ToM. Results: We found that accumulated hearing experience predicted ToM and did so indirectly through language. Also, when matched on conversational–communicative experience (i.e., accumulated hearing experience for DHH children and chronological age as a proxy for hearing children), DHH and hearing children performed equivalently on ToM. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Does the Presence of Semantic Head Facilitate Novel Word Learning in Mandarin-Speaking Children?
abstract: Purpose: Characteristics of to-be-learned words influence word learning but are understudied in Mandarin-speaking children. The current study comprehensively investigated the effect of semantic head on word learning and examined the predictive role of verbal working memory and compound awareness. Method: Fifty-nine children ( M age = 63.10 months) learned pseudo-disyllabic words with semantic head (WH words) and without semantic head (OH words). Learning was measured by four tasks (i.e., mispronunciation detection, referent identification, naming, and definition) immediately after training and by naming and definition tasks 1 day, 1 week, and 1 month after training. Results: Better learning outcomes for WH words than OH words were only observed in forming phonological representations. Significant differences were not observed between WH and OH words at all three posttraining intervals. Substitution errors in naming WH words increased 1 month after training compared to earlier time points, suggesting an interference from the OH counterparts during offline consolidation. title: A Mixed-Methods Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) Study of Implementation Outcomes of the Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS): Part 1 of a CDMS Hybrid Effectiveness–Implementation Study
abstract: Purpose: The Childhood Dysphagia Management Scale (CDMS) is a validated outcomes measure completed by evaluating therapists following instrumental swallow assessments to determine the level of follow-up care needed for children with dysphagia. We assessed the implementation outcomes of the CDMS to evaluate its readiness to be scaled out. Method: The Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance (RE-AIM) implementation science framework informed our explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. CDMS implementation outcomes were tested in a single tertiary-care children's hospital with five sites. Quantitatively , completion (number of CDMS completed/number of possible) was measured across all possible instrumental swallow assessments over a 30-month period ( N = 4,829), compared across sites and settings (inpatient vs. outpatient), measured longitudinally, and evaluated using linear mixed models across sociodemographic variables. Qualitatively , therapists ( n = 35) and referring providers ( n = 17) participated in surveys, focus groups, and semistructured interviews. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Domains of Psychosocial Risk in School-Aged Cochlear Implant Users
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study was to identify domains of psychosocial risk specific to school-aged cochlear implant (CI) users and to explain individual differences in psychosocial risk within the CI sample. Method: The parent-completed Behavior Assessment System for Children was used to measure psychosocial functioning behaviors in 59 children with CIs and 52 children with hearing 7–19 years of age. Item-level differences between the CI and hearing samples were identified, and a principal components analysis (PCA) was conducted on differentiating items to identify at-risk psychosocial behavioral constructs specific to CI users. Associations between CI-specific risk constructs and audiological, speech-language, and neurocognitive functioning were investigated. Results: CI users showed significantly greater psychosocial difficulties compared to their hearing peers on 14 items of the Behavior Assessment System for Children–Second Edition. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Reading Comprehension and Orthographic Consistency: Modeling Direct and Indirect Pathways in Children With Reading Difficulties
abstract: Purpose: This study examined how orthographic transparency shapes reading comprehension (RC) among third-grade students with reading difficulties (RD). Hebrew provides a within-language test case that features both transparent and opaque scripts, thus minimizing confounds that arise in cross-language comparisons. Method: Using path analysis, we modeled the direct and indirect associations of phonological awareness (PA), morphological awareness (MA), orthographic processing, morphosyntactic awareness (MSA), vocabulary, word reading fluency, and executive function (EF) skills with RC in each script. Participants were 231 monolingual Hebrew-speaking students with RD. Results: Results revealed that, in vowelized texts, PA had the strongest association with RC, while in unvowelized texts, cognitive flexibility, MA, MSA, and vocabulary played more central roles. Word reading fluency was associated with RC in both scripts, although the association was stronger in the opaque script. EF skills were indirectly associated with RC via linguistic and literacy pathways in both models, with cognitive flexibility additionally showing a direct association in the unvowelized condition. title: Factors Influencing Auditory Perception of Masculinity and Naturalness in Transmasculine Voices
abstract: Purpose: This study examined speaker- and listener-related factors that influence auditory perception of masculinity, naturalness, and gender attribution in transmasculine voices on hormone replacement therapy and in cisgender speakers. Method: Voice recordings were collected from six transmasculine and 12 age-matched cisgender individuals. One hundred five listeners of varying age, sexual orientation, and gender identity rated voices for masculinity and naturalness as well as attributed a gender to each voice. Speaker- and listener-related predictors of voice ratings were examined. Speaker-related factors included speaker gender, acoustic measures of voice quality, and self-report of vocal function. Acoustic measures included fundamental frequency ( F 0), smoothed cepstral peak prominence, F 0 range, Dysphonia Severity Index, and perturbation measures. Self-perceptual measures included speaker ratings of their own voice's masculinity/femininity and naturalness, as well as the Voice Handicap Index (VHI). title: Dose Considerations and Generalization Following Script Training for Poststroke Aphasia: A Randomized Factorial Clinical Trial
abstract: Purpose: Using script training as an intervention, this study modulated the dose parameters of stimulus repetition (i.e., long vs. short scripts) and session frequency (i.e., distributed vs. massed practice) and assessed their impact on maintenance and generalization in people with chronic poststroke aphasia. Method: The study was a single-site, factorial, single-blind randomized controlled trial. Participants were randomized in a 2 × 2 factorial design into one of four study arms, stratified by pretreatment aphasia severity: (a) distributed/short script, (b) distributed/long script, (c) massed/short script, and (d) massed/long script. Participants completed 10, 1-hr sessions of computer-based script training. Participants were assigned to one of four levels of script complexity with levels determined by aphasia severity. The primary generalization outcome measured performance on the trained script in a simulated conversation with a familiar speech-language pathologist posttreatment. journal_name: Journal of Speech, Language & Hearing Research
title: Phonological Skills Mediate the Association Between Left Beta/Gamma Oscillation and Reading Ability in Chinese Children
abstract: Purpose: This study aimed to investigate whether Chinese children with dyslexia exhibit atypical left-hemispheric beta/gamma oscillatory patterns during nonverbal auditory processing and to examine whether phonological skills mediate the relationship between these oscillations and reading ability. Method: Forty-two Chinese children with dyslexia and 47 typically developing controls underwent electroencephalography recording while listening to amplitude-modulated white noise (1–80 Hz). Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) was quantified over the left- and right-hemisphere regions of interest. Behavioral assessments measured reading accuracy, phonological awareness, and rapid automatized naming. Results: Compared to controls, children with dyslexia showed significantly reduced left-hemispheric beta/gamma oscillations and altered hemispheric asymmetry. Left-hemispheric ERSP was associated with reading accuracy in the dyslexia group. title: The Performance on Relative Clauses in Children With and Without Developmental Language Disorder: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: Purpose: This study attempts to quantify the magnitude of difference in relative clause (RC) performance (comprehension and production) between children with developmental language disorder (DLD) and their typically developing (TD) peers matched for age across nine languages by conducting a three-level meta-analysis. It takes sampling variance (Level 1), within-study variance (Level 2), and between-study variance (Level 3) into consideration. Method: A systematic literature search identified 25 studies investigating the performance on RCs in children with and without DLD. Data from identified studies were carefully selected and converted to Hedges's g effect sizes. Detection of outliers led to the removal of two extreme values, leaving 24 studies and 67 effect sizes for meta-analysis. title: Effects of Cognitive Load on Vocal Motor Control: A Model-Based Analysis in Individuals With Hyperfunctional and Healthy Voices
abstract: Purpose: This study examined how cognitive load (CL) influences vocal motor control by integrating acoustic measures with biomechanical trajectories derived from a model-based approach. The aim was to determine whether speakers with vocal hyperfunction (VH) exhibit distinct modulation patterns in laryngeal control compared with healthy control (HC) speakers. Method: Recordings from female speakers (63 with VH and 62 HC speakers) performing a Stroop task were analyzed. Trajectories of fundamental frequency ( f o ) and sound pressure level (SPL) were extracted and used as inputs to a computational model that estimated cricothyroid ( a CT ) and thyroarytenoid ( a TA ) muscle activations, as well as subglottal pressure ( P S ). Acoustic and model-derived measures were segmented and analyzed using mixed-effects models. Results: Significant condition effects were found across acoustic and biomechanical features, with parallel patterns in f o – a CT and SPL – P S across segments and groups.
